claims.text: A page exists in the Pulumi docs at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ (the link target of the 'Provider support policy' card on the support index page).
The Pulumi provider support policy page describes how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
The Pulumi provider support policy page identifies which Pulumi providers receive long-term security updates (i.e., some providers get long-term security updates and others do not).
The 'shield-check' icon used for the Provider support policy card exists in the docs site's icon set.

Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes pending operations currently in progress, then exits and reports the error or failure.

To perform a manual rollback after a failed Pulumi deployment, you revert the code and configuration changes of the failed deployment and run `pulumi up` to return infrastructure to its previous state.

Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state in the program against the last recorded state to determine changes.

Pulumi's not refreshing automatically before every update is an intentional design decision, because refreshing requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, adding significant latency especially for large stacks.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of the cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The Pulumi Cloud drift detection documentation exists at /docs/deployments/concepts/drift/.
The 'Refreshing state' section exists in /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/ with anchor #refreshing-state and explains refresh behavior.

A Pulumi resource's logical name is part of its auto-assigned resource URN; the logical name only needs to be unique within a stack, while the physical name (known to the cloud provider) typically needs to be unique within a certain scope, sometimes globally.
Pulumi's auto-naming creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterward (e.g., `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` instead of `my-bucket`).
Pulumi auto-naming lets Pulumi replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.

Auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis, which yields precise physical names without random suffixes but loses the benefits of auto-naming (side-by-side stacks and less-downtime replacement).
Project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has sections with anchors #autonaming and #autonaming-configuration.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program; it is the user's responsibility not to persist them outside of Pulumi without securing them.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` encrypts the configuration value so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key for every stack to encrypt that stack's secrets, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.

Because a different encryption key is used per stack, encrypting the same value in two different stacks yields different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files, so an encrypted value cannot be copied between files with a text editor and `pulumi config set` must be used instead.
When running a preview, update or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret configuration data, which is plain text during execution and accessible by any part of the Pulumi program via the config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to know what resources and parameters are available and to determine return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so users rarely need to leave their IDE when defining Pulumi programs.
Pulumi experimental features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable (such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`).
`PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true` is an environment variable that enables Pulumi experimental functionality.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When an experimental feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi focuses on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers it maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Pulumi-maintained provider major versions older than the previous major (i.e., beyond the latest major and the security-updated previous major) receive no patches at all.
The current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi can be found in the Pulumi Registry at /registry/.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.

Minor provider versions typically include new resources and features, performance improvements, and bug fixes without introducing breaking changes; the release notes for each provider release summarize new capabilities or fixes.
Updating to the latest minor version on the current major at least quarterly is the recommended practice for maintaining Pulumi provider versions.
In npm, the tilde operator (e.g., `~1.2.3`) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Provider patch versions are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
Pulumi recommends never being two or more major provider versions behind, because jumping a major version risks breaking changes and may require a multi-step upgrade.
The Provider support policy page exists at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/.
Pulumi docs pages exist at /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/ (Pulumi ESC FAQ), /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/ (Pulumi Cloud FAQ), and /docs/support/faq/policies/ (Pulumi Policies FAQ).
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
Pulumi 'actively maintains' the latest major version of every provider it publishes (maintenance-status statement).
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The providers that receive long-term support (LTS) updates on eligible older versions are: AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.

The Pulumi Registry package pages exist at /registry/packages/aws/, /azure/, /azure-native/, /azuread/, /command/, /docker-build/, /gcp/, /kubernetes/, /tls/, and /vault/ (linked from the LTS provider list); the link labeled 'Azure Classic' points to the 'azure' package and 'Azure AD' points to 'azuread'.
The LTS branch of a covered Pulumi provider ships High/Critical CVE security patches, including fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
The LTS branch of a covered Pulumi provider also ships fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch that are needed to ship the security patches.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new resources or new resource properties.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain performance improvements.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain non-security bug fixes.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi LTS provider releases remain compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless otherwise prompted by security fixes.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, exactly one long-term support major version exists per covered provider at any time.
When major version N+1 of a covered Pulumi provider ships, it becomes the new N, and the old N becomes the new LTS major.
When N+1 of a covered Pulumi provider ships, the old long-term support major reaches end of life on the same day, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the long-term support major of a covered Pulumi provider, only the latest minor version receives patches; earlier minor versions are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers who pin a Pulumi provider to a specific major version automatically receive patch releases as they ship; pinning to a specific major version is recommended.
Pinning to a specific major version of a Pulumi provider is the recommended approach for consuming LTS releases.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered Pulumi provider is the LTS version, and older majors receive no patches.
N is the latest released major version: if v3 is the newest release, then v3 is N, v2 is N−1 (LTS), and v1 and earlier are end of life.

The current major version (N) of a Pulumi provider is supported until N+1 ships, and ships new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions.

The long-term support version (N−1) of a covered Pulumi provider is supported for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships, and receives security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
End-of-life Pulumi provider versions (N−2 and older) are not supported and will not receive updates.

The Pulumi support FAQ at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ has a section 'What are the best practices for maintaining provider versions' (anchor #what-are-the-best-practices-for-maintaining-provider-versions).
The Pulumi Registry page exists at /registry/.
The 'Getting support' page exists at /docs/support/getting-support/.
